audience.notes: Australian couples in their 30s, AUD 150K+, often marrying overseas or with a family faith tradition to honour. Some are devout, some want one verse for a parent or grandparent. Tone respectful and neutral: no preaching, no theology beyond sources, no judgement of either partner's faith.

payload.search_intent: Informational: find the right verse quickly, then know how to use it (in personal vows or as a reading) without getting the legal or church side wrong.
payload.angle: The calm, sourced Australian guide: verses couples actually use, split into verses for your own vows and verses for readings, quoted from a public-domain translation with the reference linked; then what nobody else covers: the legal words you still need in Australia, how a church ceremony uses its own form, and how readings work at a destination or symbolic ceremony, where a Wedded Advisor coordinates celebrant, readers, printed order of service and timing.

outline.h2: Does the Bible contain wedding vows?
outline.answers: Is there a set biblical vow? Short answer first: there is no single word-for-word wedding vow in the Bible; the traditional vow wording comes from church services, and couples borrow verses about love and commitment.
must_include: Answer in the first two sentences (AI Overview and snippet target).

Only what sources say. Attribute the traditional 'to have and to hold' wording to church liturgy (e.g. the Book of Common Prayer) only if research confirms it; link /expert-advice/traditional-wedding-vows for the full words.
Ruth 1:16-17 context only as sourced: spoken by Ruth to Naomi, not between spouses.

outline.h2: Bible verses couples use in their vows
outline.answers: Which short verses work inside personal vows? Grouped by theme (commitment and loyalty; love in action; unity and partnership; faithfulness).
must_include: For each: book, chapter and verse; one-line public-domain text (WEB or KJV), linked to the source text at the reference; one line on why couples choose it.

Candidates seen across the SERP: Ruth 1:16-17, Song of Songs 8:6-7, Ecclesiastes 4:9-12, Genesis 2:24, Mark 10:9, Colossians 3:12-14, 1 John 4:19, Proverbs 3:3, Ephesians 4:2-3. Research confirms text and translation.
Short verses flagged as 'fits in one breath' for couples who want brevity (related search: short bible verses for wedding vows).
Never quote NIV, ESV, NRSV or NKJV text; name by reference only.

outline.answers: Which passages are read aloud in the ceremony, and how long are they?
must_include: 1 Corinthians 13:4-8 (why it is read, only as sourced), Colossians 3:12-17, Romans 12:9-18, 1 John 4:7-12, Song of Songs 2:10-13, Genesis 2:18-24, John 15:9-12.
Approximate reading length, and who usually reads (a parent, grandparent or friend): give the paying parent a role.
Link /expert-advice/which-readings-work-at-a-wedding for choosing secular and religious readings; do not repeat its advice.
Optionally cite the Church of England readings page as an official church list (official source, not a competitor).

outline.h2: How to weave a verse into your own vows
outline.answers: How do I use a verse without it sounding like a sermon?
must_include: Three patterns: open with the verse; echo one phrase as your promise; close with it.
One short worked example (original wording, not copied).
Keep within the length the parent guide gives (250 to 300 words, about two minutes); link /how-to-write-wedding-vows.
Tell your partner and celebrant or minister in advance if one of you is quoting scripture and the other is not.

outline.h2: The legal words you still need in Australia
outline.answers: If we write our own scripture-based vows, is the marriage still legal? What does a church ceremony change?
must_include: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(1): a minister of religion of a recognised denomination may use the form and ceremony recognised by that denomination; s 45(2): otherwise each party must say the prescribed words. Link legislation.gov.au at the claim.
s 46(1): an authorised celebrant who is not a minister of religion must say the monitum (the words about the nature of marriage). Link at the claim.
Reuse the legal anchor from the funny vows late pack (run-log decision); research confirms wording against the current compilation.
Church ceremonies: the minister or parish confirms the vow form and whether personal vows or chosen readings are allowed; Catholic couples link /expert-advice/catholic-wedding-vows.
The celebrant, minister or parish confirms the order of service, never the Wedded Advisor.
Answers persona fear 'planning from the other side of the world' and the legal-validity worry.

outline.h2: Readings at a destination or symbolic ceremony
outline.answers: Can we have Bible readings at a wedding overseas, and who arranges it?
must_include: Many couples marry legally in Australia and hold a symbolic ceremony abroad, where readings are free to choose; link /expert-advice/weddings-abroad-where-can-you-legally-get-married.
Some civil ceremonies exclude religious content (link /expert-advice/wedding-order-of-service, which states this; research must confirm which countries before naming any).
Italy example: civil, Catholic and symbolic rites differ; link /destination-weddings/civil-ceremony-in-italy-vs-catholic-and-symbolic-rites and /destinations/europe/italy.

Invisible work a Wedded Advisor coordinates: briefing the celebrant or priest on readings, readers' travel and rehearsal, printed order of service, microphones outdoors, wet-weather backup for the ceremony site, translation for local guests.
Answers persona fear 1 (wrong local supplier) by showing the advisor's vetted network, without overclaiming.
